h1: Pint, schooner or half and choosing serve sizes for a taproom
title: Choosing Serve Sizes for a Taproom | Craft Beer School
desc: What pints, schooners and halves actually hold, how serve sizes affect price, waste and guest choice and how to pick the right pours for an Indian taproom.
teaser: A pint is 568 ml in London, 473 ml in New York and whatever the menu says in Bengaluru.
standfirst: Serve sizes look like a small menu decision. They shape what guests try, how much you earn per litre and how much beer goes down the drain. Here is how to choose them.
sections:
Beer serve sizes have names that travel badly. A British imperial pint is 568 ml and a half pint is 284 ml. An American pint is 473 ml. A schooner is a name used for different sizes in different countries; in parts of Australia it means about 425 ml. In India there is no single convention. Menus use 300 ml, 330 ml, 400 ml, 500 ml or a borrowed name.

The name matters less than the number. Print the volume in millilitres next to every serve on the menu. Guests compare prices. They deserve to know what they are buying.

Each size does a different job:

  • Taster or sample. 60 to 100 ml, to help guests choose. Usually free or close to it.
  • Small pour. Around 200 to 300 ml, for strong beers, curious drinkers and a second round that is not a full commitment.
  • Standard pour. Around 400 to 500 ml, the main sale for most styles.
  • Pitcher or tower. Sharing for groups, often at a lower price per litre.

A small pour encourages guests to try more of your range. A strong imperial stout or barleywine should rarely be served in a 500 ml glass. Our beer glassware guide covers which glass suits each style.
Price per millilitre, not per glass

Work out your price per litre for each size and make the logic visible. A small premium per millilitre on small pours is normal, because the glass, washing and service time are the same whatever the volume. Big discounts per litre on pitchers can pull your average down, so set them deliberately. Our beer pricing strategy guide explains how to build the menu prices from cost.

Keep the steps simple. Two or three sizes per beer is plenty. A menu with five sizes for each of twelve beers is a spreadsheet, not a menu.

Choose glasses that hold the stated volume with room for a proper head. A 400 ml serve in a 400 ml brim-full glass means either a flat pour or short measures. Brim-full glasses with a fill line, or lined glasses, help staff pour consistently. Measure your real pours with a measuring jug during a busy shift. Small over-pours across hundreds of serves a night add up to a lot of beer given away.

Check your state's rules too. Excise and legal metrology rules in some states set conditions on measures and pack sizes for alcohol. Ask your licensing adviser.

An office crowd on a weekday may prefer smaller pours and a quick exit. A weekend group may want pitchers. A tourist taproom may sell more flights and small pours as people explore the range. Watch your POS data for a month after any change and see which sizes sell, at what times and with which beers.

Strong beers deserve smaller default pours. It is good hospitality, it encourages responsible drinking and guests will happily try a second style. Always have alcohol-free options on the same menu.

Large serves need extra thought. A beer tower on the table warms up over an hour, especially in Indian summers, so the last glass tastes very different from the first. Pitchers lose carbonation as they sit. If you offer them, keep them to lighter, lower strength beers and smaller sizes. Consider an ice core or chilled pitcher. Price them so the discount per litre is modest.

Takeaway growlers, where your state permits them, are another serve size with their own rules on filling, sealing and labelling. Fill them cold, purge with CO2 if you can and tell guests to drink them within a day or two. A flat, warm growler is a poor ambassador for your beer.

Serve sizes touch price, waste, guest experience and even how fast kegs empty. Each feels like a small choice. Together they decide how much money a litre of beer earns. That link between the glass and the profit and loss is one of the first things a brewpub owner should get comfortable with.
faqs: How many millilitres is a pint?
A British pint is 568 ml and an American pint is 473 ml. In India there is no single standard, so menus should show the volume in millilitres.
A beer glass size whose volume differs by country. In parts of Australia it means about 425 ml.
Should strong beers be served in smaller glasses?
Yes. Smaller pours suit strong styles, show them better and encourage guests to drink responsibly.
